solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A horse hit hard — so turned to shoer?

definitions.text: A horse hit hard — so turned to shoer?

parts.note: taken as written
a nag is an old or worn-out horse
to ram is to strike with great force

explanation.surface: A horse gets a hard knock, and so gets sent off to the farrier.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: the letters of HORSE, rearranged, spell SHOER, so the horse has been ANAGRAMMED. A shoer is someone who fits horseshoes, which is why the surface feels natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearranging the letters of one word into another is exactly what the question mark hints the setter did here, turning an equine into a farrier.

clue.text: Things made apparent primarily by Irish broadcasters with info

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the opening letter of this word
RTÉ is Ireland's national broadcaster, Raidió Teilifís Éireann
information is a collection of facts

explanation.surface: Things become clear, mainly thanks to Irish TV people sharing information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Things made apparent' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'made'; 'apparent primarily' supplies a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An artefact is any object crafted by human hands, such as a tool or ornament, so it is literally something manufactured.

clue.text: Italian peeled giant onions

indicators.note: peeling strips away the outer skin, so the outside letters of the phrase are dropped to leave the core

parts.note: the letters inside, once the outer layers come off

explanation.surface: An Italian cook strips the skin off some enormous onions.
explanation.walkthrough: Two letters come off each end of 'giant onions', leaving ANTONIO running across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio is a common Italian man's name, borne for instance by the merchant in Shakespeare's play set in Venice.

clue.text: Poison bringing a temperature — turning yellow before long

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming before means sitting higher up the column, ahead of what follows

parts.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: or is the heraldic name for gold or yellow
to pine is to long or yearn for something

explanation.surface: A poisoning victim runs a fever and their skin soon goes yellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective about time but is the verb to yearn. OR, the heraldic tincture, is a crossword staple for gold or yellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Atropine is the toxic alkaloid extracted from deadly nightshade, used medically but lethal in larger doses.

clue.text: Innkeeper is married, I'm keen to emphasise

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for married
someone keen to do something does it promptly, so this becomes a first-person statement: I emphasise at speed

explanation.surface: A landlord insists on pointing out that they are married.
explanation.walkthrough: After the abbreviation for married, 'I'm keen to emphasise' is rephrased as 'I stress quickly'. The answer is Shakespeare's hostess of the Boar's Head tavern in Henry IV and Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistress Quickly runs the Boar's Head tavern in Eastcheap where Falstaff drinks, making her Shakespeare's best-known landlady.

clue.text: Tricky part of course? Company head keeps eye in

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: DG is short for director general, the head of an organisation such as the BBC
to eye someone lustfully is to ogle them

explanation.surface: A golfer asks about a hard hole, while the firm's boss keeps his eye in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eye' is a verb here, not the organ. 'Keeps eye in' sounds like staying in practice, but it means the boss holds the leering inside.
explanation.definitionFit: On a golf course a sharp bend in the fairway makes the hole awkward to play, and golfers call such a hole this.

clue.text: Mess is where you'll find the brass?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dirt, filth or a disorderly state
second meaning: from the northern English saying that where there's dirt there's money

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'where there's muck there's brass' means dirty work pays well; brass is British slang for money, not the metal or senior officers.
explanation.definitionFit: Muck is dirt or filth, and the Yorkshire proverb places money precisely in grimy, unglamorous trades.

clue.text: Yours truly on way to work organised attorney's notes

indicators.note: in a down clue, sitting on something means placed above it, ahead in the column

parts.note: yours truly is a jocular way of saying me
MO is modus operandi, a way of operating
to run an event is to organise it
a DA is a district attorney in the US; the apostrophe-s is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: I'm heading to the office, where I've arranged my lawyer's paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organised' looks like an anagram signal but is a plain synonym. 'Attorney's notes' also tempts as a single definition; the definition is just 'notes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoranda is the Latin plural of memorandum, a written reminder or informal message, so it means short written records.

clue.text: Act unexpectedly to cut fare for people in US

indicators.note: a cut goes into something, so one piece is set inside the other
an unexpected outcome is not the usual order, so these letters come out rearranged

parts.note: these three letters rearranged
chow is slang for food

explanation.surface: Someone behaves oddly to slash the prices charged to American passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' suggests a ticket price, but it means food, as in bill of fare.
explanation.definitionFit: The Choctaw are a Native American nation originally from the south-eastern United States, now centred in Oklahoma and Mississippi.

clue.text: Name briefly associated with animal sanctuary's birds

indicators.note: to put something briefly is to cut it short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a title is the name of a book or work
Noah's Ark was a refuge for animals; the apostrophe-s is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A wildlife refuge's birds get their names in short form.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ark is the classic animal sanctuary, and the possessive supplies its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Titlark is an old name for the meadow pipit, a small streaky brown songbird of open country.

clue.text: Doctor apparently banged up for a caper

indicators.note: apparently tells us to take the phrase literally, a person seemingly locked up, so one piece is shut inside another

parts.note: banged up is British slang for imprisoned, in gaol (jail)
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A physician seems to have been jailed over some prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caper' suggests a crime to go with being banged up, but here it is a playful leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a joyful skipping jump, the kind lambs make in spring, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Enjoyment to be had with daughter in pool

parts.note: fun is enjoyment
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent and daughter have a good time in the swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pool' pictures swimming, but it is money pooled together.
explanation.definitionFit: A pool is a shared stock of money contributed by several people, which is exactly what a common fund is.

clue.text: What family vet might charge for effect?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read cryptically: a flat fee for each animal treated
second meaning: the verb to carry out or bring about

explanation.surface: A family asks how much the vet will bill them for the result.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as PER-PET RATE, a charge for each animal. 'Effect' looks like a noun, but it is the verb meaning to bring about.
explanation.definitionFit: To effect something is to carry it out or cause it, and the answer means to commit or carry out a deed, usually a bad one.

clue.text: Screws not for fixing high platform

indicators.note: something that needs fixing is broken, so these letters must be put back together in a new order

parts.note: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A DIY warning: these screws aren't meant for putting up a tall stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For fixing' sounds like the job the screws are meant for; it actually tells you the letters are broken and need reassembling.
explanation.definitionFit: A crow's nest is a lookout post fixed near the top of a ship's mast, a small raised perch for a sailor.

clue.text: Tedious don, I go on a bit!

indicators.note: in a down clue, pieces that go on are placed after, one below the next

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on and wear them
taken as written
some is a portion, a bit

explanation.surface: A dull university lecturer confesses to rambling on a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' pictures an Oxbridge lecturer, but it is the verb meaning to put on clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something so dull and repetitive that it tires and bores you.

clue.text: Keen on keeping West thus divided?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: to be into something is to be keen on it
W is the abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: A political question: does enthusiasm for the West leave the country split?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen on' is the informal sense of 'into', as in being into jazz.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cut or split into two halves has been separated, so the phrase describes a thing divided down the middle.

clue.text: Passed a range we know south of plain

indicators.note: in a down clue, south of something means below it, so later in the column

parts.note: overt means plain, open to view
taken as written
ken is the range of one's knowledge, what we know

explanation.surface: A traveller crosses a familiar mountain range lying south of the flatlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' and 'plain' suggest geography, but a range here is a scope of knowledge and plain means obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: A car that has been passed on the road by another vehicle has been overtaken, so the two are synonyms in the motoring sense.

clue.text: Maybe miss each mail that's gone astray

indicators.note: something gone astray has wandered from its proper place, so the letters are out of order

parts.note: eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Perhaps you'll fail to receive every letter that got lost in the post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe miss' reads as a verb, perhaps failing to get something, but it is a noun: a girl, and 'maybe' flags an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Michaela is a girl's name, so a young woman addressed as Miss might be one example of it.

clue.text: Small spot on ermine

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
spot on means exactly right, to a T

explanation.surface: A tiny mark on a white fur robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot on' is read together as the phrase 'to a T'; the surface splits it into a mark lying on something.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine is the name given to this animal, and its fur, when its coat turns white in winter.

clue.text: Demanding one stops travelling by cab

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a taxing task is demanding
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Being difficult, a passenger halts the taxi ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' looks like halting, but it means plugging a gap, as a cork stops a bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb 'to taxi' can mean to ride in a hired car, so going by taxi in this sense gives the present participle.

clue.text: Excellent being on leave in a NE region of France

indicators.note: in an across clue, being on something means following it, placed to its right
in means inside, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: A1 means excellent, with the 1 written as the letter I
to quit is to leave
taken as written
taken as written: northeast

explanation.surface: A fine thing to be on holiday in a corner of north-east France.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places the region in the north-east, but Aquitaine is in the south-west; 'a NE' is just letters. A1 becomes AI because the digit 1 resembles the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquitaine is a historic province and modern region in south-western France, around Bordeaux.

clue.text: Reserve acquired by old company head

parts.note: ICI was Imperial Chemical Industries, a British chemicals giant broken up in the 2000s
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Orford Ness

explanation.surface: Spare cash is taken over by the former boss of a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' suggests stock or savings in a business surface, but it means a cool, aloof manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Reserve as a personality trait is emotional coolness or distance, and a frosty, standoffish manner is often called icy.

clue.text: Climber on ascent skirting top of glacier's torn skin

indicators.note: in a down clue, ascending means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards
to skirt something is to go round its edge, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a liana is a woody climbing vine of tropical forests

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, so only that one is used

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: A mountaineer climbing around a glacier's edge rips some skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' pictures a mountaineer, but it is a plant; reversed, its letters wrap round the one taken from the glacier.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnail is a hangnail, a small painful strip of loose skin that tears away beside a fingernail.

clue.text: Snuff out of metal box good for everyone? Rather!

parts.note: ex is Latin for out of, as in ex-directory
a tin is a metal container
G is the abbreviation for good
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, suitable for all ages
-ish means somewhat, rather

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether tobacco from a tin is good for all, and gets an enthusiastic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snuff' suggests powdered tobacco and 'Rather!' an old-fashioned yes, but snuff is the verb and rather means somewhat.
explanation.definitionFit: To snuff a candle is to put out its flame, so the two are synonyms for dousing a light or fire.

clue.text: County in need of pole for flag

indicators.note: being in need of something means lacking it, so a letter is missing

parts.note: The abbreviation for Wiltshire, a county in south-west England
S for south, one of the poles

explanation.surface: A county needs a flagpole to fly its banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' and 'flag' suggest a flagpole, but pole is a compass point and flag is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to droop or lose energy, just as a plant does when it lacks water.

clue.text: Shrub of note with instant appeal

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
a mo is a moment, as in 'half a mo'
SA is sex appeal

explanation.surface: A notable bush that looks good straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of note' reads as 'distinguished', but note is a musical note. SA for sex appeal is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimosa is a flowering bush or small tree of the acacia family, with fluffy yellow blossom.

clue.text: Thoughtless fool going on a bender?

indicators.note: in an across clue, going on something means placed after it

parts.note: a knee is a joint that bends
a jerk is a stupid person

explanation.surface: A reckless idiot heads off on a drinking binge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bender' suggests a drinking spree, but it is read literally as something that bends.
explanation.definitionFit: A reflexive reaction made without consideration is described this way, after the automatic kick of the leg when tapped below the kneecap.

clue.text: Giant blunder on field concerning

parts.note: an OG is an own goal, a blunder on the football pitch
re means concerning, about

explanation.surface: A huge error made about some farmland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant' looks like an adjective for the blunder, but it is the noun and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a huge, man-eating monster of fairy tales, so it is a kind of giant.

clue.text: Come across non-professional sort of training?

parts.note: lay means amateur, not of a profession
hands-on training is practical, learning by doing

explanation.surface: An amateur stumbles upon a practical course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come across' looks like 'seem', as in coming across as amateurish, but it means find.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay hands on something is to obtain or locate it, just as you might find or stumble upon it by chance.
